studies.title: Long COVID: A Modified Delphi Consensus on Definition, Burden, Diagnosis and Management in Southeast Asia.
studies.authors: Burhan, Erlina, Chew, Huck Chin, Isbaniah, Fathiyah, Jogulu, Sathya Rao et al.
studies.abstract: Long COVID is a heterogeneous post-infectious condition following acute severe acute respiratory syndrome-coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection. Ongoing uncertainty around its definition, burden, diagnosis and management complicates clinical recognition and care in Southeast Asia. A modified Delphi consensus study was conducted with twelve experts from six Southeast Asian countries to develop regional guidance on long COVID. Consensus was predefined as ≥ 80% agreement, corresponding to at least 10 of 12 experts selecting the same response in multiple-choice questions or indicating agreement on Likert-scale questions (e.g. agree/strongly agree, most important/more important, relevant/highly relevant). Questions that reached consensus were removed from the subsequent round, while unresolved questions were revised, consolidated, or expanded. In the final round, a post hoc descriptive category, 'moderate endorsement', was applied to Likert-scale questions that had not reached consensus, with 'important' as the midpoint category of the five-point importance scale ('most important' to 'least important'), to capture responses judged important but falling short of the consensus threshold. Consensus was reached for all 'definition', 'burden' and 'management' theme questions and most 'diagnosis' questions. Experts defined long COVID as unexplained symptoms persisting for > 3 months after SARS-CoV-2 infection, distinct from post-acute COVID-19, with no minimum severity threshold requirement. Long COVID was recognised as affecting approximately 6%-10% of individuals after SARS-CoV-2 infection, consistent with published WHO and KSID estimates; clinical evaluation and symptom-guided testing were recommended for its diagnosis. Hospitalisation during acute COVID-19 was identified as a risk factor for developing long COVID. The experts recommended multidisciplinary, symptom-directed care, rehabilitation, pacing and follow-up. Vaccination and reinfection prevention were supported as important long COVID risk-reduction strategies, and early antiviral treatment should be considered to prevent severe acute illness and hospitalisation in high-risk individuals. Consensus was not reached on the past medical history required for diagnosis; moderate endorsement was observed for booster status, absence of early antiviral treatment, pre-COVID health assessment and standardised patient-reported outcome tools. This Delphi study provides a practical regional consensus framework for long COVID in Southeast Asia.

studies.title: Development and initial content validation of the Vienna post-exertional malaise questionnaire: an iterative mixed-methods study.
studies.journal: Quality of life research : an international journal of quality of life aspects of treatment, care and rehabilitation
studies.authors: Pimminger, Theresa, Ahrens-Schwabe, Annika, Fragner, Tobias, Brandl, Tobias et al.
studies.abstract: Post-exertional malaise (PEM) is a multidimensional exertion-response pattern involving diverse triggers, variable onset, and prolonged recovery. This study developed and content-validated the Vienna Post-Exertional Malaise (VPEM) Questionnaire, a patient-reported outcome measure assessing functional decline, recovery, crash-associated symptoms, and pacing adaptations in ME/CFS. An iterative mixed-methods instrument-development study combined quantitative ratings and qualitative feedback across sequential evaluation cycles. An initial 13-item draft, informed by existing PEM, fatigue, and functional-capacity instruments and consensus literature, was evaluated by individuals with ME/CFS or Post-COVID-19 syndrome (PCS) using Likert ratings, open-ended feedback, and interviews. Quantitative data were summarised descriptively, and qualitative data were analysed using deductive-inductive structuring content analysis. Revisions were documented in revision matrices. The revised instrument was evaluated by an interdisciplinary expert panel using domain-level and item-level ratings of relevance and clarity. Twelve individuals with ME/CFS and one individual with PCS fulfilling ME/CFS criteria evaluated the questionnaire. Ratings showed high approval for length (92.3%) and terminology (76.9%), while completeness and clarity were more heterogeneous. Qualitative findings identified ambiguities in distinguishing PEM from non-specific fatigue, missing trigger domains, and insufficient representation of intra-individual variability. After revision, the expert panel (n = 11) rated PEM coverage as complete or largely complete (100%) and the multidimensional structure as suitable or very suitable (90.9%). Item-level ratings showed high relevance (S-CVI/Ave = 0.96), whereas clarity ratings were more variable (S-CVI/Ave = 0.82). The VPEM Questionnaire operationalises PEM as multidimensional post-exertional deterioration. Findings support initial content and face validity, warranting further psychometric validation.

studies.title: A New Outlook on Infection-Associated Chronic Conditions and Illnesses.
studies.authors: Bertolli, Jeanne, Hinckley, Alison F, Mead, Paul S, Patel, Pragna et al.
studies.abstract: Infection-associated chronic conditions and illnesses (IACCI) encompass several debilitating syndromes with overlapping symptoms that have been identified and documented for decades, primarily following infectious disease outbreaks. Conditions following infection that are diagnosed with objective clinical tests have been relatively well characterized and accepted by the medical establishment, although the relationship to infection can be challenging to establish. In contrast, syndromes that lack objective tests, even when following a recognized infection, such as myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome, and dysautonomia, are underrecognized and often stigmatized. The COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent recognition of Long COVID as the newest example of IACCI offer new opportunities to address all aspects of IACCI. Lessons learned from the government's multi-agency public health response to Long COVID could be beneficial to ensure readiness for the long-term consequences of sporadic infections, outbreaks, and future pandemics.

studies.title: Implementation effectiveness of the Long COVID and Fatiguing Illnesses Recovery Program (LC&FIRP): a multimodal Extension for Community Healthcare Outcomes (ECHO) model for clinician learning.
studies.authors: Zuber, Alexandra, Rothwell, Jonathan T, Godino, Job G, Samaniego, Jane C et al.
studies.abstract: Long COVID and other infection-associated chronic conditions (IACC) present management challenges for primary care clinicians and often require patient access to multidisciplinary specialists. To strengthen primary care capacity, the Long COVID and Fatiguing Illnesses Recovery Program (LC&FIRP) implemented a multi-modal learning model combining Extension for Community Healthcare Outcomes (ECHO) case-based learning with complementary educational modalities. The ECHO learning component was evaluated for effectiveness in a Type II hybrid design randomized control trial, and an implementation evaluation assessed implementation of the full LC&FIRP model to inform future implementation and scale-up. We conducted a qualitatively driven mixed-methods implementation evaluation of the LC&FIRP model, assessing acceptability, feasibility, fidelity, sustainability, and scalability. Participants comprised clinicians from a federally qualified health center serving predominantly uninsured, low-income, and medically underserved patients in San Diego, CA. All trial clinicians were offered monthly webinars and quarterly asynchronous online short courses; intervention clinicians were additionally offered weekly ECHO sessions. Data sources were session surveys at the end of every session or short-course, quarterly clinician follow-up surveys, and interviews with participants, subject matter experts (SMEs) and clinic administrators at program end. Acceptability findings reflected high clinician satisfaction and perceived utility of the weekly and monthly offerings but moderate sustained engagement and negligible participation in the quarterly short courses. Clinicians valued most the interactive peer exchange; practical diagnostic and treatment approaches; and lessons from SMEs with lived experience. Feasibility barriers included competing clinical and administrative demands and the time commitment required for participation. Most program components were implemented with fidelity but fewer weekly ECHO sessions and case presentations were delivered than planned. Sustainability and scalability showed early promise with the continuation of weekly and monthly offerings after trial end, but future barriers remain. This study demonstrates that a multi-modal program combining ECHO case-based learning with complementary educational offerings may be feasibly implemented and is acceptable to clinicians for supporting primary care management of complex chronic conditions, although sustaining engagement and scaling the model will require adaptations to reduce participation burden and resource requirements.

studies.title: Treatment strategies in pancreatic adenosquamous carcinoma: a systematic review and pooled analysis of individual cases.
studies.authors: Gao, Xiang Yu, Ganatra, Nency, Abdelhakeem, Ahmed, Tran, Nugyen et al.
studies.abstract: Pancreatic adenosquamous carcinoma (PASC) is a rare 1-4% of all pancreatic cancers and an aggressive pancreatic malignancy characterized by mixed adenocarcinoma and squamous histologies. Even after surgical intervention, patients with PASC have a lower median overall survival (mOS) than those with the more prevalent pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Secondary to its rarity, there are no formal guidelines, published clinical trials, or systematic reviews on treatment strategies for managing PASC. The primary objective was to assess mOS in months among patients with local non-metastatic disease treated with different modalities. Secondary objectives were to assess differences in mOS between chemotherapy regimens and according to surgical resectability and initial tumor size, as well as to evaluate the independent association between chemotherapy and overall survival using multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression. A comprehensive search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Google Scholar, and Cochrane Library for all full-text articles up to July 2026 identified 503 studies that were conducted globally. 72 case series and reports that met inclusion criteria were selected following PRISMA guidelines. A total of 89 patients from 72 publications were included. The median age was 66 (interquartile range, 60-72) years, 49 patients were male, and the median tumor diameter was 48 (interquartile range, 35-74) mm. Forty-nine patients received chemotherapy and 55 underwent surgical resection. Eighty-eight patients had both survival time and vital status and were included in survival analyses, with 56 deaths observed. In the primary treatment-modality analysis, among surgically unresectable patients, mOS was 3.0 months with neither chemotherapy nor radiotherapy, 6.0 months with chemotherapy alone, 13.7 months with radiotherapy alone, and 15.5 months with combined chemotherapy and radiotherapy (P=0.01). Among surgically resectable patients, mOS was 10.8 months with neither chemotherapy nor radiotherapy, 6.7 months with chemotherapy alone, 4.0 months with radiotherapy alone, and 26.0 months with combined chemotherapy and radiotherapy (P=0.03). In the secondary multivariable Cox model, chemotherapy was independently associated with improved overall survival [hazard ratio (HR), 0.41; 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.24-0.70; P=0.001], while surgical resection was not independently associated with survival (HR, 1.17; 95% CI: 0.58-2.34; P=0.66). mOS across all patients was 8.0 months (95% CI: 6.5-12.0). Median survival differed significantly according to disease extent, ranging from 33.0 months among patients with borderline resectable disease to 4.0 months among patients with metastatic disease (P=0.0004). Restricted mean survival at 24 months was 15.6 months with chemotherapy versus 8.2 months without chemotherapy. The association between chemotherapy and improved survival remained significant across most sensitivity analyses. Among patients with unresectable disease, mOS was 18.0 months with S-1, 5.4 months with gemcitabine, and 4.0 months with 5-fluorouracil (P=0.09). Combined chemotherapy and radiotherapy were associated with the longest mOS among both surgically resectable and unresectable patients in the primary treatment-modality analysis.

studies.title: Persistently activated virus-specific CD8 T cells indicate antigen-driven immune aberrations in long COVID.
studies.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
studies.authors: Painter, Mark M, Reeg, David B, Douek, Naomi R, Gray-Gaillard, Sophie L et al.
studies.abstract: Long COVID (LC) affects millions of people worldwide, yet its driving mechanisms remain incompletely defined and no treatment has been approved. Persistence of SARS-CoV-2 and reactivation of herpesviruses have been implicated in LC, but direct detection of these viral antigens in blood and tissues has been challenging. T cells are exquisitely sensitive to viral antigens, survey organs throughout the body, and can be readily sampled in peripheral blood. Using high-dimensional spectral flow cytometry and single-cell sequencing approaches with multiplexed peptide/HLA tetramers, we profiled virus-specific T cells from hundreds of people with LC and recovered controls. We identified a subset of people with LC that maintained elevated activation of CD8 T cells targeting SARS-CoV-2 spike and/or lytic antigens from Epstein-Barr virus, but not other viral specificities. Spike-specific cells in LC expressed genes linked to TCR stimulation, terminal effector differentiation, and exhaustion and demonstrated reduced functionality upon cognate peptide stimulation

studies.title: Sex-Specific Plasma Proteomic Alterations Underpin Distinct COVID-19 Progression and Post-COVID-19 Condition.
studies.authors: Lu, Qiuhan, Zhang, Yi, Yi, Shiyu, Wu, Yuwen et al.
studies.abstract: Sex differences in COVID-19 and its sequelae remain poorly understood, which hinders targeted therapies. We performed plasma proteomic analyses of 69 hospitalized patients with COVID-19 and 30 healthy controls from a prospective Chinese cohort. The UK Biobank and Mount Sinai Biobank were employed for validation and provided insights into the progression mechanisms. Biological and tissue enrichment analyses characterized sex-specific pathways and tissue-enriched proteins. We identified ANXA11, a molecular tether that physically links RNA granules to lysosomal membranes to enable their long-distance transport and local translation, as a protein associated with male-specific susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 infection. Decreased ANXA11 protein levels were linked to higher risk of infection in males, replicated in the UK Biobank. Sex-specific proteomic alterations revealed distinct biological responses, including glycosylation-related pathways in females and cell adhesion, platelet-leukocyte interactions, and inflammatory responses in males. Sex-specific protein changes were also associated with distinct post-COVID-19 symptom profiles. ANXA11 was identified as a novel protein associated with the male-specific susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 infection. Sex-specific protein changes revealed distinct mechanistic differences between male and female patients in COVID-19 progression and may explain sex differences in post-COVID-19 conditions.

studies.title: Incidence and risk factors of acute respiratory illness associated with influenza, COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus within a birth cohort study.
studies.authors: Bird, Bryden, Thorn, Louise, Aminisani, Nayyereh, Wood, Tim et al.
studies.abstract: Influenza virus, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are leading causes of acute respiratory infections (ARIs). New Zealand's coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) public health measures disrupted the circulation of these viruses in 2020-2021, creating a rare opportunity to explore the impact of potential immunity gaps on age-specific infection risk. We analyzed data from 843 participants aged between 0 and 4 years enrolled in the Southern Hemisphere Influenza and Vaccine Effectiveness Research and Surveillance 3 (SHIVERS-III) birth cohort, a longitudinal community-based study in New Zealand, during 2020-2024. During the respiratory season, weekly surveillance captured ARI symptoms and severity. Nasal swabs were collected from symptomatic participants and tested for viral RNA by RT-PCR. Incidence rates (IRs) and incidence rate ratios (IRRs) were estimated for the surveillance period and adjusted for age, sex, ethnic group, socioeconomic status, and influenza vaccination status. No influenza or SARS-CoV-2 infections were detected in 2020 and 2021. From 2021 to 2024, RSV had the highest IR during the surveillance period (63.2/100 person-years [PY]; 95% CI, 56.6-69.8), followed by SARS-CoV-2 (39.3/100 PY; 95% CI, 34.5-44) and influenza (35.7/100 PY; 95% CI, 29-42.3). Age influenced infection risk: infants <6 months had the lowest incidence of influenza and RSV, potentially reflecting maternally derived immunity and limited exposure. Risk increased after 6 months of age, peaking at age 1 year for RSV and at age 2 years for influenza. Influenza vaccination lowered symptomatic influenza risk (IRR 0.66; 95% CI, 0.44-1.00). In the New Zealand community setting in the post-COVID-19 era, individual respiratory virus illness patterns differ in children aged 0-4. Influenza vaccine shows protection, and age influences virus-specific risk. Influenza virus, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are major causes of acute respiratory illness in early childhood, yet current understanding is largely reliant on hospital-based surveillance that underestimates the broader community burden. This study addresses this limitation by providing comprehensive, community-based estimates of incidence, severity, and symptom profiles across these viruses within a single longitudinal birth cohort. By leveraging the unique epidemiological context created by pandemic-related disruptions, it offers important insights into how changes in exposure influence subsequent infection risk and virus circulation. The direct comparison of three major respiratory viruses within the same population highlights distinct age-related risk patterns and disease characteristics. In addition, our research provides real-world evidence of the reduced risk of influenza-associated acute respiratory illness among vaccinated children. These findings strengthen the evidence base for age-targeted immunization strategies and improve understanding of early-life respiratory virus epidemiology.

studies.title: A novel model demonstrating that human immune cells promote multiorgan SARS-CoV-2 dissemination and human T cells limit anti-viral innate immunity.
studies.authors: Wolabaugh, Amber, Agashe, Vrushali V, Wang, Zicheng, Danzl, Nichole M et al.
studies.abstract: Despite extensive studies, many questions remain regarding the pathology and mechanisms behind Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), and particularly on post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC). Because existing mouse models cannot recapitulate human immune responses, we developed a human immune system (HIS) mouse model with physiologic expression of hACE2.

studies.title: "I Picked Myself Up Through Prayer and Soups": Factors Impeding and Enhancing Long COVID Recovery Among Latinos in South Texas.
studies.authors: Alvarez-Hernandez, Luis R, Clark, Loren C, Uzoh, Hemma, Gonzales, Xavier F et al.
studies.abstract: We aimed to understand what factors have impeded and enhanced Long COVID recovery among Latinos in South Texas. Through community partners, 78 participants were part of seven focus groups. We analyzed the data following Braun and Clarke's Reflexive Thematic Analysis. Factors that impeded recovery were: (1) Working while ill due to labor needs, expectations, and limited safety nets, (2) Mistrusting health care due to invalidating systemic barriers, (3) Grieving former self, and (4) Obsessing over the known and unknown. Factors that enhanced recovery were: (1) Focusing on a conscious fight to preserve life, (2) Leveraging cultural knowledge to reconnect with their sense of wholeness as a person, (3) Choosing Western medicine as one method of healing, and (4) Relying on God and trusted ones. Long COVID recovery interventions among South Texas Latinos must account for structural and social determinants of health and cultural ways of healing.

studies.title: Converging pathomechanisms link SARS-CoV-2 infection with major neurodegenerative diseases.
studies.authors: HeFeng, Feng Q, Martí-Sarrias, Andrea, Guvenilir, Heval Atas, de Sá, Renata Baptista Vieira et al.
studies.abstract: Neurological complications are among typical clinical manifestations, both during the acute phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection and long-term post-acute COVID-19 sequelae, i.e., Long COVID. A growing body of evidence connects SARS-CoV-2 infection to systemic inflammation, peripheral immune dysregulation, functional alteration of the blood-brain barrier (BBB), neuroinflammatory processes, mitochondrial dysfunction and pathological protein aggregation, all of which are central to the pathogenesis of major neurodegenerative diseases. In this review, we discuss the converging shared underlying molecular mechanisms that link the 'acute' SARS-CoV-2 infection that often only lasts for days and 'chronic' neurodegenerative diseases that often take decades to develop. We further review human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs)-derived brain organoid and BBB models for Parkinson's disease (PD) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) as well as artificial intelligence (AI)-facilitated knowledge graph methods that are used to hypothesize and validate the potential mechanistic links. We propose that besides the established links between viral infections and neurodegenerative or neuroinflammatory conditions, such as Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) in multiple sclerosis or herpes zoster in AD, SARS-CoV-2 infection might be another important factor driving the future burden of the most common neurodegenerative diseases.

studies.title: Metformin and Severe Post-COVID-19 Outcomes Among Individuals With Diabetes Mellitus.
studies.authors: Dozier, Zachary B, Wang, Lin-Chiun, Ji, Yunwen, Anzalone, A Jerrod et al.
studies.abstract: We evaluated the relationship between metformin, one of the most commonly prescribed medications for individuals with diabetes, and COVID-19 sequelae. We evaluated a retrospective cohort of individuals in the National Clinical Cohort Collaborative with Type 2 diabetes mellitus and COVID-19 who were prescribed metformin or a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor (DPP4i) at least 30 days before the onset of acute COVID-19 between 1 October 2021, and 15 November 2023. We compared the 12-month cumulative incidence of Long COVID diagnosis (ICD-10 U09.9: Post COVID-19 condition, unspecified), probable Long COVID (based on a model-derived phenotype), and mortality between individuals prescribed metformin versus DPP4i. We applied Super Learner and targeted maximum likelihood estimation to obtain risk ratios while adjusting for covariates of interest. In our sample of 53 332 individuals with Type 2 diabetes and COVID-19, we found that metformin prescription was associated with a lower risk of all-cause mortality after COVID-19 (adjusted risk ratio [aRR]: 0.61, 95% CI: 0.51, 0.73). We also observed that metformin users, compared to DPP4i users, had a slightly lower risk of probable Long COVID (aRR: 0.87, 95% CI: 0.81, 0.94) but did not detect a significant relationship with the clinically defined outcome of Long COVID diagnosis (aRR: 0.90, 95% CI: 0.68, 1.20). These findings support the hypothesis that metformin prescription during acute COVID-19 may be associated with lower mortality among adults with diabetes.
