studies.title: Receptor-binding autoantibodies are not associated with post-COVID fatigue.
studies.authors: Achleitner, Martin, Dänhardt, Juliane, Kardashi, Romina, Toepfner, Nicole et al.
studies.abstract: Persistent fatigue is a common symptom following SARS-CoV-2 infection, but its underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Autoantibodies targeting G-protein coupled receptors and other neurotransmitter-related receptors have been proposed as potential biomarkers or mediators of post-COVID symptoms. However, their association with post-COVID fatigue remains unclear. Therefore, in the current study, we investigated receptor-binding autoantibodies against 13 neurotransmitter-related receptors in 206 participants with prior infection with SARS-CoV-2. Three groups of patients were enrolled: controls with no persistent fatigue, patients experiencing new-onset post-infection fatigue, and a group of patients who already suffered from fatigue before their infection with SARS-CoV-2. Fatigue was assessed using a standardized self-reported fatigue questionnaire. We found no significant differences in the concentrations of the measured receptor-binding autoantibodies between participants with new-onset fatigue, pre-existing fatigue, and controls without persistent fatigue. In multivariable analyses, none of the individual antibody concentrations was significantly associated with new-onset fatigue after adjustment for age, sex, and time since infection and correction for multiple testing. Individual antibody concentrations were also not associated with fatigue severity. The proportion of participants exceeding manufacturer-defined reference values did not differ significantly between the study groups. Similarly, cumulative antibody positivity was not associated with fatigue severity. In conclusion, in this cohort of SARS-CoV-2-infected participants, we found no evidence that concentrations of the measured receptor-binding autoantibodies are associated with post-COVID fatigue or fatigue severity. These findings do not support the use of these antibodies as stand-alone biomarkers of post-COVID fatigue. Because all participants had previously experienced SARS-CoV-2 infection, the study cannot determine whether infection itself alters antibody concentrations. Furthermore, the binding assays do not establish whether the detected antibodies have functional receptor activity. These findings underscore the urgent need for longitudinal studies with comprehensive clinical phenotyping and functional antibody assays are needed to further investigate the potential role of receptor-binding autoantibodies in post-COVID symptoms.

studies.title: Persistent COVID-19 Symptoms in General Population and Healthcare Workers: Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis.
studies.authors: Boufleuer, Eduarda, Vieira, Tainara Wink, Sakamoto, Victória Tiyoko Moraes, Anschau, Fernando et al.
studies.abstract: COVID-19 can cause persistent symptoms that continue after the infection, condition known as long COVID. This study aimed to identify the prevalence of persistent signs and symptoms of COVID-19 in individuals with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection and among healthcare workers. This is a systematic review with meta-analysis guided by PRISMA and registered in PROSPERO (CRD42023460632). Cohort studies with a minimum follow-up of 12 weeks after COVID-19 infection were included. Searches were conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Scielo, and LILACS/BVS databases and gray literature, in November 2023. Rayyan was used for article selection, and pooled prevalence meta-analysis for each symptom was conducted in R. Methodological quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. A total of 2,456 studies were identified, with 59 articles included in the systematic review and 58 in the meta-analysis, comprising 196,863 participants. The symptoms with the highest pooled prevalence (95% CI) were fatigue (0.29[0.24-0.36], 95% PI: 0.05-0.78) and dyspnea (0.16[0.12-0.22], 95% PI: 0.01-0.71). Healthcare workers showed lower prevalence rates for some persistent symptoms (fatigue, dyspnea, cough, taste changes, and gastrointestinal symptoms) than the general population. Most studies were of fair quality. Despite the findings of a high prevalence of persistent symptoms, high heterogeneity remained a key limitation.

studies.title: Low-dose prednisolone and B vitamins for post-COVID-19 syndrome in Germany: the PreVitaCOV randomised clinical trial.
studies.authors: Gágyor, Ildikó, Klug, Andreas, Schwager, Alexander, Gelbrich, Götz et al.
studies.abstract: Post-COVID-19 syndrome is burdensome and not yet adequately treatable, with persistent symptoms including fatigue, dyspnoea, and cognitive impairment. The Pan American Health Organisation recommends rigorous evaluation of potentially beneficial interventions. We investigated the efficacy and safety of prednisolone and vitamins B1, B6, and B12 in patients with post-COVID-19. This randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (2 × 2 factorial design) was conducted in adults with post-COVID-19 at three university sites in Germany. Adult patients with persistent symptoms after a documented SARS-CoV-2 infection ≥12 weeks ago and without acute COVID-19, major comorbidities, pregnancy or breastfeeding, prior intensive care treatment for COVID-19, recent use of trial drugs, or potentially interacting concomitant medications were included. From January 13, 2023 until July 25, 2024 participants were randomly assigned to 28 days of once-daily oral treatment with prednisolone (20 mg on days 1-5, 5 mg on days 6-28), B vitamins (thiamine nitrate [B1], 100 mg, pyridoxine hydrochloride [B6] 50 mg, and cyanocobalamin [B12] 500 μg), prednisolone and B vitamins, or placebo. The primary outcome was change in overall symptom severity from baseline to day 28, assessed in the intention-to-treat population (participants who received at least one dose of study drug) at the first follow-up visit after randomisation with a customised Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) total T-score. A change of ≥3 points was considered clinically meaningful. Efficacy was assessed using a pre-specified factorial analysis of the main effects of prednisolone and B vitamins. Safety was assessed by analysing frequency and severity of adverse events in all randomised patients (safety population). This completed trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05638633). Of 2498 patients assessed for eligibility, 323 were randomised and 310 patients had evaluable data for the outcomes. The mean age was 44 (standard deviation (SD) 13) years, 200 participants were women. The mean change in PROMIS T-score was -4·3 (SD 5·1) with prednisolone, -3·2 (SD 5·0) with B vitamins, -4·5 (SD 4·5) with prednisolone plus B vitamins, and -2·9 (SD 4·6) with placebo. The adjusted mean difference between participants treated with prednisolone and those not treated was -1·4 points (95% confidence interval (CI), -2·5 to -0·4; p = 0·008), driven primarily by the change in the fatigue subscore (-6·4 points, p < 0·001). B vitamins showed no statistically significant or clinically meaningful difference compared with no B vitamins (adjusted mean difference (MD), -0·1 points; 95% CI, -1·2 to +1·0; p = 0·85). Adverse events were equally distributed between groups, with no study-drug-related serious adverse events. This trial showed a statistically significant short-term reduction in symptom severity in the five dimensions of the PROMIS score in patients with post-COVID with low-dose prednisolone. However, the effect did not reach the prespecified threshold for clinical relevance. Further research is needed to confirm the efficacy of prednisolone and to determine the optimal dose and treatment duration while balancing benefits against longer-term adverse effects. studies.title: Post-COVID Gastrointestinal Symptoms and Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction: A Focus on Persistent Diarrhea.
studies.authors: Saheb, Fauz
studies.abstract: Persistent gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms after SARS-CoV-2 infection include diarrhea, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, constipation, nausea, and other disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBIs), but these entities should not be treated as interchangeable. In a meta-analysis of long-COVID studies, any GI symptom was reported in approximately 22% of patients and diarrhea in 10%, although heterogeneity was very high. In a large US Veterans Affairs cohort, post-acute COVID-19 was associated with incident diarrhea (hazard ratio {HR}: 1.58, 95% CI: 1.52-1.65; excess burden 7.99 per 1,000 persons at one year) and irritable bowel syndrome (HR: 1.54, 95% CI: 1.28-1.86). Prospective Rome IV cohorts report lower absolute rates of formally diagnosed DGBIs; one study found persistent DGBI symptoms in 6.6% at six months, with functional diarrhea in 2.2% and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) in 2.5% at three months. Mechanistic evidence supports intestinal involvement during acute infection and demonstrates associations with epithelial/angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) perturbation, immune activation, barrier dysfunction, altered microbial taxa, and impaired microbial metabolite production. However, persistent viral RNA or antigen, dysbiosis, and gut-lung signaling remain proposed or associative mechanisms rather than established causes of chronic diarrhea. Treatment evidence specific to post-COVID functional diarrhea is sparse. A large synbiotic trial improved a broad "gastrointestinal upset" domain in post-acute COVID syndrome, but did not enroll a defined chronic diarrhea or Rome-positive population; probiotic and fecal microbiota transplantation trials showing GI effects were largely conducted during acute COVID-19. Therefore, current care should first exclude organic and medication-related causes, then apply phenotype-based management extrapolated from established diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D) and functional-diarrhea practice while clearly acknowledging the limited post-COVID-specific evidence. Standardized definitions, pre-infection GI data, appropriate controls, functional microbiome measures, and dedicated randomized trials are priorities for future research.

studies.title: Real-world evidence speaks louder than biological plausibility. Editorial on "Ursodeoxycholic acid and long COVID in steatotic liver disease: a nationwide cohort study".

studies.title: SARS-CoV-2-specific monoclonal antibody AER002 in Long COVID: an exploratory randomized phase 2a mechanistic trial.
studies.authors: Peluso, Michael J, Ryder, Dylan, Dalhuisen, Thomas, Chu, Danny Hoi Tsun et al.
studies.abstract: Persistence of SARS-CoV-2 has been proposed as a biological driver of Long COVID, a disabling chronic illness with no proven treatments. We conducted an exploratory, placebo-controlled, double-blind, 2:1 randomized mechanistic trial (NCT05877508) of the SARS-CoV-2-specific monoclonal antibody AER002 in 36 participants who met the World Health Organization case definition of Long COVID. After baseline characterization, participants received a single infusion and were followed for 360 days. The primary endpoint was the PROMIS-29 Physical Health Summary Score (PHSS) at 90 days; secondary and exploratory endpoints included patient-reported and objective measures of physical and neurocognitive function as well as blood-, imaging-, and tissue-based biomarkers. While AER002 was safe and well tolerated, no significant differences in physical health, quality of life, objective measures of physical function or cognition, or blood-based biomarkers were demonstrated between the treatment and control arms. In a post-hoc analysis, participants with a lower baseline SARS-CoV-2 antibody level and higher drug exposure were more likely to perceive treatment benefit based on the Patient Global Impression of Change scale (p < 0.05 for anti-S, S1, and RBD). Although AER002 was not efficacious in this proof-of-concept study, our findings could inform future trials using monoclonal antibodies to target viral persistence in Long COVID.

studies.title: Metformin at the Time of COVID-19 Infection and Risk of Long COVID: A Target Trial Emulation Study.
studies.authors: Bramante, Carolyn T, Stürmer, Til, Huling, Jared D, Buse, John B et al.
studies.abstract: Our objective was to evaluate metformin prescribed at the time of SARS-CoV-2 infection on the risk of developing Long COVID (LC) in electronic health record data. We conducted a new user analysis of metformin prescribed within 6 days of documented infection with severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) versus experimental control: prescription for fluvoxamine, fluticasone, ivermectin, or montelukast. a clinic visit in the 0-6 months and the 6-12 months before infection. metformin or control within 12 months. LC or death (LC/D), to address death as a competing risk, among patients prescribed drug within Days 0-6 of infection. LC was defined by diagnosis code or computable phenotype. We used entropy balancing to estimate the average treatment effect with a weighted log-linear model. After weighting, there were 248 in the metformin and control groups; the average age was 53 (16); 16% were Black; and 16% were Hispanic. In the primary analysis, 10/248 (4.0%) in the metformin group developed LC/D versus 21/248 (8.5%) in the control group, adjusted risk ratio (aRR) 0.47 (95% CI 0.25-0.89, p = 0.02). For prescriptions on Days 0-1 relative to infection, aRR was 0.39 (95% CI 0.12-1.24); for prescriptions on Days 0-14, the aRR was 0.75 (95% CI 0.52-1.08). In this observational analysis, metformin prescribed within a week of documented SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with a 53% lower risk of LC over 6 months than comparator medications. With the aRR of 0.47 (95% CI 0.25-0.89), any risk reduction between 75% and 11% is highly compatible with our data. This analysis of electronic health record diagnoses is important for the reproducibility of clinical trial results that ascertained the same outcome but via participant-report.

studies.title: Evaluation of COVID-19 antibodies with demographic profiles, vaccination, and infection.
studies.authors: Chandra, Tulika, Singh, Vijay Kumar, Bharti, Jyoti, Agarwal, Devisha et al.
studies.abstract: COVID-19 infection has raised concern regarding the short duration of immunity afforded by vaccines and antibodies elicited by natural infection. This aim was to examine differences in antibody titers associated with age, sex, vaccination doses, and infection in healthcare workers with previous positive quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction tests. Antibodies detection by the enzyme-linked immunoassay (ELISA) was validated by electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (ECLIA) to find a cost-effective antibody test. studies.title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Systematic Literature Reviews in Metabolic Phenotyping: A Methodological Framework and Validation Study.
studies.authors: Cox, Maartje, Osorio Mosquera, Javier, Khandaker, Shaimaa, Sala, Samuele et al.
studies.abstract: Systematic literature reviews are widely acknowledged to be at the top of most evidence hierarchies but are very time-consuming and labour-intensive. The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) offers possibilities to accelerate the review process. We propose a systematic literature review protocol that incorporates AI and evaluate the accuracy of AI against a human-constructed gold standard. Human researchers performed a systematic literature review on the PubMed metabolomic literature investigating Long COVID. OpenAI model o3-mini was then used via the application programming interface to carry out the three key stages of a systematic literature review: 1) screening articles for inclusion criteria, 2) evaluating articles' risk of bias (RoB) using a customised metabolomics tool based on well-established quality criteria, and 3) extracting data from articles. The performance of AI was evaluated against a manually created reference by the assessment of accuracy, negative predictive value, precision, sensitivity, specificity, F1 score, and Cohen's kappa. Out of the 320 identified articles, 33 met all inclusion criteria. AI performed screening, RoB assessment, and data extraction with mean accuracies of 92.7% ± 4.9%, 91.9% ± 5.9%, and 92.0% ± 9.2%, respectively, in ~ 10 h and at a cost of ~ 15.35 USD, while human reviewers took ~ 116 h, equivalent to ~ 2000 USD at minimum wages, to complete these steps in duplicate. OpenAI model o3-mini can independently complete the three main stages of systematic literature reviews in the metabolomics domain, thus considerably reducing the time to complete such reviews, at minimal cost. Nonetheless, human reviewers should always verify the AI-generated output to ensure robustness. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s43657-026-00336-y.

studies.title: Self-reported long COVID associated with sleep problems and poor sleep quality among adults in Germany: results of the German Health Update 2023 (GEDA 2023).
studies.authors: Beyer, Ann-Kristin, Yessimova, Dinara, Kümpel, Lisa, Eckert, Grit et al.
studies.abstract: Long COVID refers to various long-term health impairments following a SARS-CoV-2 infection, including physical, cognitive, and psychological symptoms. Sleep problems are among the most prevalent neuropsychiatric symptoms of long COVID and can negatively affect daily functioning and quality of life. This study aims to investigate sleep onset problems, problems maintaining sleep and poor sleep quality in associations with long COVID among adults in Germany. Analyses are based on data from the cross-sectional nationwide telephone interview survey "German Health Update" (GEDA 2023). Between March 2023 and February 2024, 9,310 adults (50.8% female, median age = 60.8 years) answered questions on any prior SARS-CoV-2 infection and long COVID status, as well as on sleep onset problems, problems maintaining sleep and poor sleep quality over the past 4 weeks. Weighted prevalence estimates for each sleep variable were calculated by self-reported SARS-CoV-2 infection and long COVID status. Multivariable logistic regressions were conducted, adjusted for age, sex, level of education, chronic conditions, depressive symptoms, COVID-19 vaccination status, and multiple SARS-CoV-2 infections. Participants with self-reported current long COVID reported higher proportions of sleep onset problems (32.6%), problems maintaining sleep (47.8%) and poor sleep quality (44.8%) compared to participants without a SARS-CoV-2 infection (20.0%, 30.8 and 24.1%, respectively) or prior infected participants without long COVID (13.8%, 23.8 and 20.0%, respectively). In multivariable logistic regression analyses, participants with self-reported current long COVID had an increased likelihood of experiencing problems maintaining sleep (adjusted odds ratio (aOR) = 1.73; 95% CI = 1.23-2.44) and a higher likelihood of poor sleep quality (aOR = 1.81; 95% CI = 1.29-2.55) compared to non-infected individuals; however, sleep onset problems were not associated with long COVID. Our findings from general population data suggest that adults with current long COVID have 1.7- to 1.8-fold higher odds of problems maintaining sleep and poor sleep quality than non-infected individuals. Given the potential impact on quality of life and physical and psychological functioning, sleep-related symptoms may represent an important target for clinical assessment and management in individuals with long COVID.

studies.title: Single-cell transcriptomics uncovers persistent hepatic immunometabolic remodeling following SARS-CoV-2 infection in obese hosts.
studies.authors: Qian, Wei, Wei, Xiaoqin, Park, Soo-Jeung, Garcia Diaz, Josefina et al.
studies.abstract: SARS-CoV-2 infection affects multiple organs, and chronic post-viral tissue injury is often associated with persistent immune dysregulation. Obesity and related metabolic disorders are major risk factors for severe COVID-19 and post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC), including liver dysfunction. To define hepatic responses during post-acute infection, we studied lean and diet-induced obese mice at 7 and 28 days following infection with mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2. Compared with lean mice, obese mice exhibited persistent lung inflammation and fibrosis, along with liver injury characterized by increased lipid accumulation, cellular apoptosis, and metabolic dysfunction. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed obesity-associated alterations in hepatic immune and metabolic programs during post-acute infection. In particular, hepatic macrophages in obese mice showed sustained inflammatory and metabolic transcriptional alterations, while hepatocytes displayed altered programs associated with gluconeogenesis and lipid metabolism. Endothelial cells also exhibited persistent transcriptional changes linked to immune activation and prothrombotic pathways. These alterations remained evident at 28 days post-infection, suggesting incomplete restoration of immune and metabolic homeostasis in obese liver. Collectively, our findings reveal persistent obesity-associated hepatic immunometabolic remodeling following SARS-CoV-2 infection and identify cellular and molecular programs that may contribute to post-acute liver sequelae in metabolically compromised hosts.

studies.title: Glycemic dysregulation and insulin resistance across acute and post-acute COVID-19: a systematic review and meta-analysis of etiologic and prognostic evidence.
studies.authors: Muñoz-Carrillo, José Luis, Gutiérrez-Coronado, Oscar, Lopez-Hernandez, Edrei, Rodríguez López, Sandra Estefanía et al.
studies.abstract: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) can disrupt glucose regulation through inflammation, adipose-tissue dysfunction, impaired insulin signaling, and variable β-cell compensation. These evidence domains remain incompletely integrated. To synthesize evidence on glycemic dysregulation and insulin resistance or insulin sensitivity across acute and post-acute COVID-19, including metabolic trajectories and associations with adverse clinical outcomes. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect were searched. Eligible studies evaluated glucose regulation and at least one insulin-resistance or insulin-sensitivity measure during or after COVID-19. Etiological and prognostic evidence was analyzed as related but distinct domains. Prognostic meta-analysis evaluated study-defined acute hyperglycemic phenotypes; insulin-resistance or insulin-sensitivity assessment was a study-level eligibility criterion rather than part of a participant-level composite exposure. Unadjusted risk ratios (RRs) from event counts were pooled using restricted maximum-likelihood random-effects models with Hartung-Knapp adjustment. Non-combinable evidence was synthesized according to Synthesis Without Meta-analysis principles. Risk of bias was assessed using design-appropriate tools, and certainty was evaluated with GRADE. The protocol and analytical plan were retrospectively registered in OSF on August 21, 2026 (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/K5FWU). Twenty independent studies represented by 23 reports. Acute hyperglycemic phenotypes were associated with increased short-term all-cause mortality (four studies; 1,079 participants; RR 2.09, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.21-3.64; I Study-defined acute hyperglycemic phenotypes were associated with adverse COVID-19 outcomes in studies that also assessed insulin resistance or insulin sensitivity. These unadjusted estimates should not be interpreted as effects of a combined phenotype or as causal associations. Persistent metabolic abnormalities occurred heterogeneously, supporting standardized participant-level definitions and controlled longitudinal studies. https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/K5FWU, identifier 10.17605/OSF.IO/K5FWU.

studies.title: Real-world effectiveness of Paxlovid in protecting Long COVID for outpatient adult patients: A target trial emulation study from the RECOVER Initiative.
studies.authors: Zang, Chengxi, Li, Haoyang, Khullar, Dhruv, Zhang, Yongkang et al.
studies.abstract: Paxlovid (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir) has been approved for use in patients who are at high risk for severe acute COVID-19 illness. Evidence regarding whether acute use of Paxlovid protects against Post-Acute Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC), or Long COVID, is mixed in high-risk patients and lacking in low-risk patients. With a target trial emulation framework, we evaluated the association of Paxlovid treatment within 5 days of SARS-CoV-2 infection with incident Long COVID and hospitalization or death from any cause in the post-acute period (30-180 days after infection) using electronic health records from the Patient-Centered Clinical Research Networks (PCORnet) RECOVER repository. The study population included 497,499 SARS-CoV-2 positive patients between March 1, 2022, to February 28, 2023. For those who had at least 1 risk factor for severe COVID-19 illness, 159,659 were treated with at least one dose of Paxlovid within 5 days since infection and 272,048 were not treated with Paxlovid or other COVID-19 treatments during the acute infection period. Compared with the non-treated group, Paxlovid treatment was associated with reduced risk of Long COVID with a Hazard Ratio (HR) of 0.88 (95% CI, 0.87 to 0.89) and absolute risk reduction of 2.99 events per 100 persons (95% CI, 2.65 to 3.32). For those without documented risk factors, the associations (HR, 1.03, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.11; risk increase 0.80 events per 100 persons, 95% CI -0.84 to 2.45) were inconclusive. High-risk, nonhospitalized adult patients with COVID-19 who were treated with Paxlovid within 5 days of SARS-CoV-2 infection had a lower risk of Long COVID and all-cause hospitalization or death in the post-acute period. However, Long COVID risk reduction with Paxlovid was not observed in low-risk patients.

studies.title: Stem Cell Educator Therapy for Ex Vivo Immune Modulation of Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells in Patients with Long COVID.
studies.authors: Zhao, Yong, Veysman, Boris, Huang, Zhi Hua, Mendoza, Noelle et al.
studies.abstract: Long COVID, generally defined as clinical symptoms persisting for 3 months or longer following severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection, affects multiple organs and systems. At least 400 million people globally are living with long COVID, with symptoms including persistent fatigue and brain fog. Currently, long COVID care mainly consists of symptomatic management and supportive approaches, with no validated effective treatments available that address the underlying inflammation. Stem Cell Educator (SCE) therapy is a treatment developed to modulate immune responses. This protocol describes SCE therapy and its application in patients with long COVID to evaluate safety, clinical outcomes, and immunological changes. During SCE therapy, a patient's peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) are collected by leukapheresis and co-cultured with adherent cord-blood-derived multipotent stem cells (CB-SC) in vitro, after which the "educated" PBMC are returned to the patient's circulation via infusion. SCE therapy has previously been evaluated in clinical studies for type 1 diabetes and other autoimmune diseases. Twenty-five patients with long COVID (15 males and 10 females) received SCE therapy. Five patients experienced mild adverse effects during apheresis, and one patient reported itching during infusion. Brain fog and fatigue disappeared in 21 of 25 patients following treatment, and most participants reported feeling refreshed, energized, and mentally clear. Flow cytometry demonstrated reductions in inflammatory markers, including interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β)-positive cells and C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 16 (CXCL16)-positive cells. These findings demonstrate the application of SCE therapy in patients with long COVID and provide preliminary clinical and immunological observations supporting further evaluation of this approach.

studies.title: Neighborhood-Level Non-Medical Factors Alone Poorly Predict Proxy PASC Phenotype : Limited Performance of Logistic Regression and XGBoost Models.
studies.authors: Ellis-Gilliam, Amirah, Rivera-Mariani, Felix, Chen, Chuming, Zhang, Zughi et al.
studies.abstract: Early in the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, acute mortality and hospitalization showed marked disparities across socially disadvantaged groups. In some cases, individuals who initially tested positive for Post-Acute Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC) also began to experience lingering symptoms after initially recovering from SARS-CoV-2. At the time of the 2023 BRFSS survey the CDC defined PASC as self-report of any symptoms lasting ≥3 months at the time of interview that were not present before having COVID-19. An estimated 6.7% of Delaware adults self-reported symptoms consistent with PASC and 24.5% of those Delawareans reported significant activity limitations. This condition is a chronic disease and the Delaware State Health Improvement Plan (SHIP) has established a priority outcome to reduce the risk of chronic diseases. One of the goals of SHIP is to promote a combination of methods to support and identify chronic diseases and support healthy outcomes, these goals tie directly to non-medical health factors. Although there are notable poverty, food insecurity and health care access disparities at the county level in Delaware, it remains unclear whether neighborhood-level non-medical health factors alone can identify areas with high PASC prevalence so those the most in need can receive targeted resources to address this chronic condition. To evaluate whether combined ZCTA-level non-medical health factors, without patient-level clinical predictors, can discriminate against a machine-learning-derived PASC phenotype. We defined a proxy PASC outcome via a validated ML-derived probability score. established by Pfaff et al. using N3C data. This model used a variety of data points from individuals who sought care at PASC clinics and assigned each individual a score that estimated the probability of a PASC diagnosis. Our cohort was run through this same model to identify individuals with PASC. We analyzed 4,521,889 adults with SARS-CoV-2 in N3C. PASC status was assigned using the probability model developed by Pfaff et al., which incorporates clinical attendance, symptoms, comorbidities, and healthcare utilization, with a cutoff ≥ 0.90. The predictors included neighborhood-level race-ethnicity, income, socioeconomic status, education, and insurance variables; composite risk scenarios were evaluated using logistic regression and XGBoost. Logistic regression performed at chance levels (AUC ~ 0.50). XGBoost showed limited test-set discrimination (AUC 0.685 - 0.689), but cross-validated performance was weak (CV AUC 0.516-0.523) and severity for PASC was poor (recall 0.05-0.06). Neighborhood-level non-medical health factors alone were insufficient to discriminate the proxy PASC phenotype at the individual level. Considering the state of Delaware's documented county level disparities in poverty and healthcare access, future predictive models should integrate clinical characteristics, comorbidity burden, and biomarkers at the individual level. This method would more accurately identify those at risk of developing PASC and support equitable resource allocation in the communities that are most impacted by this chronic disease.

studies.title: From past to present and toward the future: a mechanism-informed clinical framework for COVID-19-associated headache and post-viral pain.
studies.authors: He, Cheng, Xue, Yan, Liu, Yao, Xu, Zhou-Can et al.
studies.abstract: Headache is a prominent acute and persistent neurological manifestation of COVID-19, representing both as a significant clinical challenge and a valuable model for understanding the neurotropic effects of SARS-CoV-2. This review synthesizes evidence showing that the epidemiology of COVID-19 headache is distinctly shaped by younger age, female sex, and a prior history of headache disorders; its clinical phenotypes are diverse, strongly associating with chemosensory dysfunctions such as anosmia; and its core pathophysiology involves neuroinflammation (e.g., cytokine-mediated pathways), trigeminovascular activation, and sex-specific neuroendocrine-immune interactions. Although acute headache often responds to conventional analgesics, persistent cases-a major component of Post-Acute Sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC)-necessitate a multidisciplinary management approach. This contrasts with the typically self-limiting headache following vaccination. Future research should prioritize longitudinal studies to define chronicity, mechanistic investigations into sex-specific pathways, and the development of phenotype-specific, personalized therapeutic strategies.

studies.title: Associations between salivary HHV-6 and long COVID severity in a cross-sectional, case-control analysis.
studies.authors: Laxton, Claire S, Tabachnikova, Alexandra, Cooke, Lily, Wang, Kexin et al.
studies.abstract: Reactivation of human herpesviruses (HHVs), particularly EBV, is associated with more severe acute SARS-CoV-2 infection and the development of Long COVID (LC). Reactivation of HHVs has been previously implicated in hormonal dysregulation, which has also been observed in LC, suggesting a potential link. This study aims to examine the relationship between LC symptoms and salivary HHV DNA, cortisol, testosterone, and oestradiol levels. Our cross-sectional, case-control study enrolled 45 participants with LC, and 45 age-sex-matched controls. Surveys and validated health questionnaires were used to collect demographics, medical history, and symptom profiles. Saliva was self-collected at waking, 15, 30, and 45 min, and 8 and 16 h after waking, across two consecutive days. Salivary cortisol, testosterone and oestradiol were measured, and extracted nucleic acid was tested for EBV, HSV 1/2, HCMV and HHV-6 A/B using multiplex qPCR, and for SARS-CoV-2 and RNaseP using RT-qPCR. Detection of salivary EBV and HHV-6 DNA copies was highest early in the morning. There were no significant differences in salivary cortisol, testosterone, or oestradiol, or in EBV or HHV-6 DNA between the LC and control groups. However, salivary HHV-6 DNA levels were positively associated with a greater aggregated LC propensity score (r = 0.24, 95% CI = 0.02-0.44, p = 0.015, adj. p = 0.030), as well as anxiety (β = 0.69, 95% CI = 0.02-1.36, p = 0.045) and depression (β = 0.24, 95% CI = 0.05-0.42, p = 0.013) scores. The observed correlation between salivary HHV-6 DNA and symptom severity suggests HHV-6 may contribute to post-acute disease, though mechanisms remain unclear. While we did not identify a relationship between salivary EBV DNA and LC, EBV may still play a role at earlier time points in the disease course, or in compartments not sampled in this study. These findings highlight the potential importance of HHV-6 in LC pathophysiology and underscore the need for longitudinal, multi-compartment studies of herpesvirus reactivation in LC. This work was supported in part by the Else Kröner Fresenius Prize for Medical Research 2023 (to AI), the Howard Hughes Medical Institute Collaborative COVID-19 Initiative (to AI), and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute (to AI), the Polybio Research Foundation (to AI and DP) and the Steven and Alexandra Cohen Foundation (to DP). National Institutes for Health (NIH) funding sources supported AT, SB and CM.

studies.title: "The past is never dead; it's not even past"
studies.journal: Journal of infection and public health
studies.authors: Spaziante, Martina, Cervoni, Matteo, Sönnerborg, Anders, Zazzi, Maurizio et al.
studies.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic has left a deep mark on healthcare systems and society worldwide. In this context, the project "European Cohorts of Patients and Schools to Advance Response to Epidemics" (EuCARE), responding to an emergency request from the European Union under the Horizon Europe programme, addressed the pandemic from different perspectives. It investigated the clinical impact of emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants, the performance of vaccines and diagnostics, post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC), schooling and vaccine hesitancy. This short report combines a review of project outputs with a consultation of the ten project principal investigators and work package leaders, all of whom responded; no formal qualitative analysis was applied. The primary objective was to identify the operational and methodological challenges encountered during EuCARE and to explore their implications for the design and implementation of future pandemic research. Investigators reported four challenges requiring coordinated action at national and European level: fragmented ethics and regulatory procedures; difficulty in rapidly mobilising specialised personnel; vaccine hesitancy and other aspects of behavioural preparedness; and vulnerable diagnostic supply chains. From these experiences we derived six "pills of preparedness": evidence-based science, workforce surge capacity, data collection and management, specialised professional roles, collaborative networks, and evidence-based communication. These lessons derive from a single consortium and from the self-reported experience of a limited number of investigators, and should be interpreted accordingly.

studies.title: Post-COVID neurological manifestations are associated with neuroinflammation, increased autoantibody burden, and persistent complement activation.
studies.authors: de Deus, João Victor Carvalho, Santos, Heloisa Ferreira Pinto, da Silva, Michele Fernanda Borges, Mamani, Roxana Flores et al.
studies.abstract: Neurological manifestations represent commonly persistent features of post-COVID conditions (PCC), but mechanisms underlying their pathogenesis remain unclear. In this study, participants with neuro-PCC (n = 29), mostly presenting with persistent headache, fatigue, sleep disturbances, anosmia/dysgeusia, cognitive complaints, and/or paresthesia, recovered from COVID-19 (n = 32), and non-infected controls (n = 32), all matched for sex and age, had paired serum samples from acute phase (0-14 days) and two time points of convalescence (3-6 months and 9-12 months) assessed for antinuclear antibodies (ANA), antibodies to extractable nuclear antigens (ENA), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), and autoantibodies against cytokines using Luminex assays. Biomarkers of neuroinflammation, including neurofilament light chain (NfL), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), total Tau protein, and neurogranin were quantified by Ella ELISA and complement activation was determined by increased C5b-9 levels. Patients with neuro-PCC showed a greater number of neurological symptoms during acute phase, with increased frequency of headache and fatigue, and a higher prevalence of obesity and cardiovascular comorbidities. GFAP remained elevated for up to one year after infection, independently of symptom persistence. However, only patients with neuro-PCC exhibited a transient increase in NfL levels during acute phase, and persistent complement activation throughout follow-up. No specific autoantibody was associated with neuro-PCC, but these patients exhibited a higher cumulative autoantibody burden. Multivariable logistic regression analysis showed that hospitalization and the neurological burden during the acute phase were associated with neuro-PCC, whereas anti-cytokine autoantibody counts showed an inverse trend. Increased complement activation and a higher autoantibody burden suggest a broad and nonspecific immune activation that may contribute to a sustained low-grade neuroinflammatory state, potentially driving the persistence of neurological symptoms after COVID-19.

studies.title: Revised estimates of types and duration of long COVID symptoms based on claims records from 245 million US patients.
studies.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
studies.authors: Nilforoshan, Hamed, Reisler, Julia, Jahanparast, Erfan, Moor, Michael et al.
studies.abstract: COVID-19 has been reported to cause multisystem effects lasting years [Z. Al-Aly, E. Topol, Science 383, 830-832 (2024)]. These findings are primarily based on cohort studies comparing test-positive COVID-19 patients to controls without known COVID-19 infection, tested or untested [M. Cai, Y. Xie, E. J. Topol, Z. Al-Aly, Nat. Med. 30, 1564-1573 (2024)]. However, such comparisons can be biased by the reasons people were tested. Using 14.4 billion insurance claims from 244.7 million US patients, we find that most long-term effects attributed to COVID-19 by unrestricted control designs likely reflect bias due to selective testing of individuals with non-COVID conditions, causing long-term effects of those conditions to be misattributed to COVID-19. We removed this bias by analyzing only tested individuals, comparing test-positive to test-negative patients. Across 614 clinical outcomes followed over 2 y, the test-based design resulted in 83.5% fewer symptoms being attributable to COVID-19 between 30 to 119 d after infection (43 attributable symptoms vs. 262 for the unrestricted control design), a 98.2% reduction at 120 to 359 d (5 vs. 286), and a 100% reduction at 360 to 719 d (0 vs. 369). The unrestricted control design also attributed unrelated outcomes (e.g., firearm injuries) to COVID-19 at a high rate, whereas the testing-based design did not. The test-based control design may modestly underestimate some effects. This study does not indicate that symptoms beyond one year are not genuine but that their attributability to COVID-19 is uncertain.

studies.title: Effects of Telerehabilitation on Quality of Life, Physical Capacity, and Symptom Burden Within the Post-COVID-19 Condition: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
studies.authors: Huang, Xiaojing, Tang, Yidan, Liu, Dongsen, Burns, Ryan Donald et al.
studies.abstract: Post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) is characterized by persistent symptoms and functional limitations that impair quality of life, and rehabilitation is an important component of its management. Because access to conventional face-to-face rehabilitation may be limited, telerehabilitation has emerged as an accessible alternative. However, the effectiveness of telerehabilitation across clinical outcomes remains uncertain, and the influence of different delivery modes is not well understood. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of telerehabilitation on health-related quality of life (HRQoL), physical capacity, and symptom burden in adults with PCC, and to determine whether delivery mode (synchronous, asynchronous, or hybrid) modified these effects. Seven databases (PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase, EBSCO, and PEDro) were searched for randomized controlled trials published from January 2020 through December 2025. Eligible trials enrolled adults with PCC and compared telerehabilitation with usual care or another control condition. The primary outcome was HRQoL; secondary outcomes included functional capacity assessed by the 6-minute walk test and sit-to-stand test, dyspnea, fatigue, and symptoms of anxiety and depression. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool. Mean differences or standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% CIs were pooled using random-effects models with the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman adjustment. Heterogeneity was quantified using I² and τ², with 95% prediction intervals reported where estimable. Certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) approach. A total of 22 randomized controlled trials involving 2294 participants were included. Telerehabilitation was associated with significant improvements in HRQoL (SMD 1.26, 95% CI 0.07-2.45; P=.04), dyspnea (SMD 1.95, 95% CI 0.60-3.31; P=.005), and functional aerobic capacity (6-minute walk test : mean difference 77.79 meters, 95% CI 30.44-125.14; P=.001). Fatigue was also significantly reduced (SMD 0.89, 95% CI 0.16-1.62; P=.02), but no significant effects were observed for lower-limb strength (sit-to-stand test: SMD 0.55, 95% CI -0.15 to 1.25; P=.12) or symptoms of anxiety and depression (SMD 0.12, 95% CI -0.13 to 0.38; P=.36). No significant differences between delivery modes were observed for HRQoL (P=.93), functional aerobic capacity (P=.29), or dyspnea (P=.16). A significant subgroup difference was observed for lower-limb strength (P=.02). Telerehabilitation may improve quality of life, aerobic capacity, and symptom burden in PCC and offer an accessible option for post-COVID rehabilitation, although the certainty of evidence was generally limited. Asynchronous delivery appears feasible for general reconditioning, whereas its benefit for lower-limb strength and the value of synchronous supervision remain uncertain. studies.title: Control-Anchored QUBO Clustering Reveals Control-Distant Postural Control Patterns in Motion Capture Balance Signals After COVID-19.
studies.authors: Kunapinun, Alisa, Nowak, Andrzej, Ellison, Peter J, Pelah, Mattan et al.
studies.abstract: Post-COVID-19 balance and postural control alterations have been reported after SARS-CoV-2 infection, but individual-level phenotyping remains challenging because post-acute sequelae are heterogeneous and often lack clear clinical ground truths. We analyzed motion capture balance data from 140 participants, including 114 post-COVID-19 participants and 26 control-group participants, who completed sensory organization/postural balance tasks under single-task and cognitive dual-task conditions. Relative joint angle trajectories were transformed into 0-5 Hz frequency-domain spectra, from which 13 balance-derived task contrasts were constructed to capture cognitive dual-task versus single-task differences, closed-eyes versus open-eyes task condition differences, and related task condition changes. Joint-wise spectral contrast features were encoded using a vector-quantized variational autoencoder. Control-distant subgroup discovery was then formulated as a control-anchored, graph-based QUBO clustering problem and solved using a quantum annealing workflow. Simulated annealing and tabu search were applied to the identical BQM/QUBO formulation as classical solver-level references, whereas Gaussian mixture modeling was retained as an unconstrained classical clustering reference. Consistent with the control-anchored design of the QUBO objective, QUBO clustering identified a selective subset of post-COVID-19 participants with control-distant latent balance profiles while largely preserving the control-group reference structure. Across all task contrasts, quantum annealing assigned 1 of 307 control-group participant-contrast assignments (0.3%) and 118 of 1366 post-COVID-19 participant-contrast assignments (8.6%) to the control-distant group. Simulated annealing and tabu search produced slightly larger but similar control-distant post-COVID-19 subsets, assigning 143 of 1366 post-COVID participant-contrast assignments (10.5%) and 0 of 307 control-group participant-contrast assignments (0.0%) to the control-distant group. In contrast, GMM assigned 63 of 307 control-group participant-contrast assignments (20.5%) and 266 of 1366 post-COVID-19 participant-contrast assignments (19.5%) to the control-distant group. Parameter sensitivity analysis showed high overall assignment agreement for the same BQM/QUBO formulation, but the exact membership of the sparse control-distant subset was more variable. Simulated annealing sensitivity analysis showed overall agreement of 98.3-100.0% and control-distant Jaccard indices of 0.836-1.000 relative to the baseline, whereas a representative QPU sensitivity analysis showed overall agreement of 93.6-100.0% and control-distant Jaccard indices of 0.443-1.000. Frequency band profiles further suggested that QUBO-derived control-distant assignments corresponded to contrast-dependent and exploratory interpretable postural control patterns, particularly in low-frequency postural sway-dominant and mid-low-frequency postural control bands. These findings support the feasibility of objective-driven, control-anchored QUBO-based quantum-assisted clustering for exploratory subgroup discovery in heterogeneous, label-limited biomedical datasets. The proposed framework does not establish diagnostic criteria for long COVID or evidence of quantum speedup but provides a hypothesis-generating approach for interpretable post-COVID-19 neuromotor phenotyping and related medical data analysis applications.

studies.title: Resveratrol for Post-COVID-19 Cognitive Dysfunction: From Molecular Basis to Clinical Translation.
studies.authors: Martinez-Fierro, Margarita L, Gonzalez-Delgado, Samantha, Solis-Hernandez, Israel A, Rocha-Pizaña, Maria Del R et al.
studies.abstract: Post-COVID-19 condition can include persistent cognitive symptoms, commonly described as impaired attention, memory difficulties, slowed processing, and "brain fog." Clinical and translational evidence implicates systemic inflammation, neurovascular dysfunction, blood-brain barrier disruption, glial inflammatory responses, oxidative stress, and altered synaptic or network function; their relative contributions remain uncertain and may differ across patient subgroups. Resveratrol is a polyphenolic compound that modifies inflammatory, redox, metabolic, endothelial, and antiviral pathways in experimental systems. This focused narrative review examines whether those actions provide a mechanistic basis for the use of resveratrol in post-COVID-19 cognitive dysfunction. Evidence was considered according to biological proximity to the intended indication, distinguishing human post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC) studies from acute-COVID-19, non-COVID-19 clinical, animal, organoid, and cell-based evidence. The review identifies candidate neurovascular, immune, and metabolic processes, evaluates where resveratrol evidence intersects with those processes, and distinguishes molecular observations from clinical questions that remain to be tested for to define the therapeutic potential of using resveratrol to treat post-COVID-19 cognitive impairment.

studies.title: Fibroid-like Uterine Lesions and Fibroid-Associated Structural Changes in a Long-Term Murine Hepatitis Virus-1 Model.
studies.authors: Jayakumar, Arumugam R, Ramamoorthy, Rajalakshmi, Patel, Urja C, Ruiz-Caordero, Roberto et al.
studies.abstract: The number of patients with long COVID continues to rise as COVID-19 persists, yet research on its implications for female reproductive health remains scarce. Long COVID is linked to an increased risk of abnormal uterine bleeding, heavier menstrual flow, prolonged periods, and breakthrough bleeding. We therefore examined whether uterine changes occur in an animal model of long COVID. Female A/J mice were inoculated with murine hepatitis virus strain 1 (MHV-1), a murine coronavirus model used to investigate long COVID-like sequelae, and a subset of infected mice received the synthetic peptide SPIKENET (SPK). Mice infected with murine hepatitis virus strain 1 (MHV-1) showed chronic uterine inflammation and myometrial changes exhibiting fibroid-like features one year post-infection. We also observed changes in α-SMA, desmin, h-caldesmon, and vimentin staining, suggesting a myometrial origin for the lesions. Further, we found pathological changes that include hyperplastic foci in the outer layer of the myometrium, a uterus with intraluminal proteinaceous fluid, and a circumscribed, round-to-oval focus of benign hyperplastic myometrium with spindle nuclei and eosinophilic cytoplasm, with interspersed small, round lymphocytes and plasma cells, consistent with mild chronic inflammation. MHV-1-inoculated mice also showed an oviduct with several lymphocytes located toward the lumen, as well as a uterus with an ectatic lumen, inspissated intraluminal fibrinoid material, and mild-to-moderate subendometrial chronic inflammation (with scattered small lymphocytes). Additionally, immunofluorescence showed increased expression of conventional and unconventional uterine fibroid markers, including PLP1, versican, PR-A, PR-B, MSH2, TGF-β1 and 3, IGF-1, CA125, and HMGA2. Serum biomarker analysis showed increased IGF-1 levels but not increased levels of the other proteins identified by immunofluorescence. Furthermore, histopathology showed no uterine fibroid-like lesions in MHV-1-inoculated mice treated with the synthetic peptide SPK (known to prevent MHV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 infection in animals). Moreover, SPK prevented increases in the above-mentioned fibroid markers as measured by immunofluorescence and partially reduced IGF-1 expression in the serum. These findings suggest that uterine fibroids may develop during long COVID in humans.

studies.title: Beyond Neuroinflammation: Targeting the Microbe-Barrier-Brain Axis Through Precision Nutrition in Neurological Long COVID (Neuro-PASC).
studies.authors: Velázquez De Castro-Bono, Amador, Castro-Luna, Gracia, Guil-Guerrero, José Luis
studies.abstract: Post-acute Neurological Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (Neuro-PASC) contribute substantially to Long COVID-related disability, with cognitive impairment, chronic fatigue, dysautonomia, and neuropsychiatric symptoms among its most debilitating manifestations. Although its pathogenesis remains incompletely understood, evidence implicates persistent immune activation, intestinal barrier dysfunction, microbiota dysbiosis, microbiome-derived metabolic alterations, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neuroimmune interactions in sustaining neuroinflammation and neurological impairment. This narrative review examines precision nutrition as a potential pathway-oriented strategy for Neuro-PASC. We synthesise evidence linking the gut microbiota, intestinal permeability, immunometabolic pathways, mitochondrial function, and neurological outcomes, while evaluating nutritional interventions targeting these mechanisms. We focus on candidate biomarkers, including serum zonulin, fatty acid-binding protein 2 (FABP2), faecal short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), and the kynurenine-to-tryptophan ratio, which may support patient stratification and personalised nutritional strategies. We also propose a stepwise framework involving dietary stabilisation, functional foods, targeted supplementation, and microbiome-based interventions, alongside practical considerations for post-exertional symptom exacerbation, dysautonomia, and mast cell-related symptoms. Finally, we identify priorities for future research, including multi-omics integration, artificial intelligence, digital health, and biomarker-stratified randomised controlled trials. Because current evidence remains predominantly observational and mechanistic, precision nutrition should be considered a complementary strategy requiring rigorous clinical validation.
